quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Both "aroma" and "of" end and begin with vowel sounds. Listen for an extra consonant sound that sneaks in between them.
quests.explanation: This is intrusion: a sound appears between two vowels even though it isn't written anywhere. In "aroma of", an intrusive /r/ bridges the gap, purely to avoid an awkward vowel collision.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "find" ends in a clear consonant sound, and "out" starts with a vowel. What happens to that consonant when you say them together naturally?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in a consonant meets a word starting with a vowel, the consonant shifts to open the next syllable instead of closing the first. In "find out", the final consonant of "find" links smoothly onto the vowel that begins "out".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Between "flat" and "pack" sits a consonant under pressure to match its neighbor. What does it become?
quests.explanation: This pairing is a classic assimilation example: the /t/ ending "flat" adopts the bilabial quality of the sound in "pack", surfacing as /p/ in natural, connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This isn't a case of a sound vanishing from "road" — it's still there, just different. What does /d/ turn into before the bilabial sound in "block"?
quests.explanation: Notice that the /d/ ending "road" isn't deleted the way it would be in elision — it survives, just transformed into /b/ to match the bilabial sound beginning "block".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /n/ at the end of "seven" is about to meet a velar sound in "goals". Does it hold firm, or shift to match?
quests.explanation: Before a velar consonant, /n/ commonly shifts to match its place of articulation. In "seven goals", /n/ becomes /ŋ/ — the sound itself changes, it doesn't disappear.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "true or" without a pause. Two vowel sounds are about to collide — what does English insert to smooth the transition?
quests.explanation: Because "true" ends in a vowel and "or" begins with one, English speakers instinctively insert /w/ between them. It's not in the spelling of either word — it's added on the fly to keep the speech flowing.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This 'r' is real — it's written into "summer" — but often silent. Listen for it specifically at the boundary with "afternoon".
quests.explanation: Speakers keep the /r/ silent in "summer" only until a vowel gives it a reason to surface. "afternoon" provides exactly that vowel, so the /r/ links the phrase together.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Unlike a sound added from nowhere, the /r/ here is already part of "for"'s spelling. What triggers it to reappear before "everyone"?
quests.explanation: This linking /r/ is predictable from spelling alone: any r-final word behaves this way before a vowel, and "for everyone" is a clean example of it.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "neighbor" ends in a silent 'r' on its own. Say it together with "and" — does that silence hold, or break?
quests.explanation: Because "neighbor" ends in 'r', the connected-speech rule is simple: pronounce the /r/ whenever a vowel follows, as it does before "and". That's what makes this linking rather than intrusion.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "good game" at natural speed. Listen right at the boundary — does the /d/ stay a /d/, or does it become something else?
quests.explanation: This is regressive assimilation: a sound changes to become more like the sound that follows it. Here, the /d/ ending "good" turns into /g/ because "game" begins with a velar consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Check the spelling of "degree" before "of" — does it end in a letter that would predict a /j/ sound? If not, where's that /j/ actually coming from?
quests.explanation: Unlike linking, where the connecting sound is already written into the word, this /j/ in "degree of" comes from nowhere in the spelling. That's exactly what makes it intrusive rather than a genuine linking sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Vowel sounds rarely bump directly into each other in fluent English. What extra sound bridges "ready" and "or" here?
quests.explanation: Two vowel sounds meeting head-on is hard to say smoothly, so speakers add /j/ as a natural bridge. You'll hear it in "ready or", even though neither word's spelling contains it.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Rather than pronouncing /d/ then /j/ separately, fluent speakers coalesce them. What do you actually hear in "hold your"?
quests.explanation: Notice that neither the original /d/ nor /j/ survives on its own — they combine into /dʒ/. That fusion is what makes "hold your" sound natural and fast.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In casual speech, does the final /t/ of "worked" get pronounced before "late", or does it just vanish?
quests.explanation: English speakers simplify clusters like this one by deleting a stop consonant rather than forcing it in. The /t/ in "worked" is the one that goes missing before "late".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen at natural speed: does "trust your" keep two distinct consonant sounds at the boundary, or blend them into a new one?
quests.explanation: In relaxed, natural speech, /t/ and /j/ rarely stay separate at a word boundary like this one. They coalesce into /tʃ/, exactly as in "trust your".
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's no /r/ anywhere in the spelling of "China". Yet something links it to the vowel that opens "and" — what is it?
quests.explanation: This inserted /r/ has no basis in spelling — it exists purely to smooth the vowel-to-vowel transition between "China" and "and". That's the hallmark of intrusion.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen carefully between "play" and "and". An unwritten sound appears purely to ease the vowel-to-vowel transition. Which one?
quests.explanation: Native speakers automatically fill the gap between two vowel sounds with /j/, even when there's no letter to justify it. "play and" is a clear example of this intrusive sound.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a spelling trap: "review" looks like it should flow straight into "again", but a sound gets inserted that isn't written anywhere. Can you hear it?
quests.explanation: Since "review" doesn't end in a written consonant that could explain a /w/, the /w/ you hear before "again" is added by the speech system itself — an intrusive sound, not a spelled one.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A velar consonant is coming up in "cousins". What does that do to the /n/ just before it in "ten"?
quests.explanation: Speakers save effort by letting /n/ anticipate the velar sound ahead. So in "ten cousins", /n/ is pronounced as /ŋ/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Because "there" is spelled with a final 'r', a vowel right after it — like the one starting "is" — can bring that /r/ back into speech. Listen for it.
quests.explanation: The /r/ you hear between "there" and "is" isn't invented — it's the word's own final letter reactivated by the vowel that follows, which is the textbook definition of linking /r/.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /d/ ending "bad" to the velar sound that opens "grade". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /d/ becomes /g/ in "bad grade" to match the velar consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "cool off" as one smooth unit, not two separate words. Where does the final consonant of "cool" end up?
quests.explanation: This is linking: the consonant isn't added, dropped, or changed — it simply moves to attach to the following vowel. That's exactly what happens between "cool" and "off".
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "should" and the /j/ starting "yell" don't survive as separate sounds in fast speech. What do they turn into together?
quests.explanation: This is why "should yell" doesn't sound like two crisp, separate words: the boundary consonant /d/ and the /j/ of "yell" merge into the single sound /dʒ/.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "doctor" already has a written 'r' at the end — normally silent before a pause, but what happens to it right before the vowel that opens "appointment"?
quests.explanation: "doctor" ends in a written 'r' that's silent in isolation (in non-rhotic pronunciation) but reappears whenever a vowel follows. Because "appointment" begins with a vowel, the /r/ resurfaces — this is linking /r/, not intrusion, since the letter is genuinely there in "doctor".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "your own" naturally. That final 'r' in "your", usually silent, resurfaces here — why, do you think?
quests.explanation: This is linking, not intrusion, because the 'r' is already written into "your". It stays silent before a pause or consonant but comes back to life right before the vowel that opens "own".
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The consonant at the end of "put" has a vowel waiting right after it in "it". Does it stay attached to "put", or slide onto the next syllable?
quests.explanation: Fluent English resyllabifies across word boundaries whenever a consonant meets a vowel. Here, the last sound of "put" glides directly into "it", making the phrase sound like one continuous unit.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen to the boundary between "watch" and "out". A consonant and a vowel are meeting — what does fluent speech do with them?
quests.explanation: Rather than pausing between the consonant and the vowel, speakers connect them directly — the consonant essentially becomes the first sound of the next syllable. You hear this clearly in "watch out".
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In natural speech, a word-final consonant followed by a vowel often gets pulled into the next syllable. Does that happen between "hang" and "on"?
quests.explanation: This smooth consonant-to-vowel connection is what makes native speech sound joined-up rather than word-by-word. "hang on" links this way naturally.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Picture how a native speaker would say "send flowers" in a fast, everyday sentence. Is every single consonant still there?
quests.explanation: This is a textbook case of consonant-cluster elision: the /d/ between two consonants is dropped to keep speech fluent and effortless in "send flowers".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ in "select" is trapped between two other consonants right before "size". What usually happens to a stop consonant stuck in that position?
quests.explanation: Rather than pronounce all three consonants back to back, speakers cut the /t/ from "select" entirely. The result flows straight from the first consonant into "size".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.
